lead: A real symmetric matrix equals its transpose. Covariance matrices, graph adjacency matrices, and stiffness matrices are symmetric. For such matrices, eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal, so one orthogonal matrix Q diagonalizes A. This is orthogonal diagonalization. It turns coupled equations into independent directions. Engineers use it for principal axes, vibration modes, and data alignment. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic; the calculation is short, but the normalization rules are strict.
prereq: You need: eigenvalues and eigenvectors from 4.1, diagonalization from 4.4, and Gram-Schmidt from Unit 5.

blocks.text: For a real symmetric matrix A, the spectral theorem gives three facts. Every eigenvalue is real. Eigenvectors from different eigenvalues are orthogonal. There is an orthonormal basis of Rⁿ made of eigenvectors of A.
The proof of orthogonality uses the dot product. For symmetric A, (A x)ᵀ y = xᵀ(A y). Put A x = λ x and A y = μ y. Then λ xᵀy = μ xᵀy, so (λ − μ)xᵀy = 0. If λ ≠ μ, then xᵀy = 0.

This is stronger than ordinary diagonalization. A general real matrix may have complex eigenvalues, and may have too few real eigenvectors to form a basis. A real symmetric matrix always has a full set of real eigenvectors, and they can be made perpendicular.
Arrange orthonormal eigenvectors as columns of Q. Then QᵀQ = I, so Q is orthogonal. Put matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of D. Then QᵀAQ = D, equivalently A = QDQᵀ.

items: For each eigenvalue, find a basis of its eigenspace, the null space of A − λI.
If an eigenvalue repeats, apply Gram-Schmidt inside that eigenspace.
Put these vectors as columns of Q; put eigenvalues in the same order in D.
Check QᵀQ = I and QᵀAQ = D.

blocks.text: Column order in Q must match diagonal order in D. Swapping both is allowed; swapping only one changes the product.

blocks.where: Q is orthogonal with orthonormal eigenvectors as columns; D is diagonal with eigenvalues in matching order.

figure.caption: The flow from a real symmetric matrix to a diagonal form. The two guarantees are real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenspaces; Gram-Schmidt is needed only when an eigenvalue repeats.

spec.title: Symmetric spectral theorem
spec.aria: For a real symmetric matrix, eigenvectors from different eigenspaces are orthogonal; normalizing them gives Q with Q transpose A Q diagonal.

examples.question: Orthogonally diagonalize A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: find an orthogonal Q and a diagonal D with QᵀAQ = D.
steps: Check QᵀQ = I (columns are unit and perpendicular), so Q is orthogonal.
Check QᵀAQ = D directly: AQ = QD = [[1/√2, 3/√2], [−1/√2, 3/√2]], so QᵀAQ = D. This follows from matching eigenvectors to diagonal entries, not from QᵀQ = I alone.
examples.check:
import math
A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]
tr = A[0][0] + A[1][1]
det = A[0][0]*A[1][1] - A[0][1]*A[1][0]
disc = tr*tr - 4*det
l1 = (tr - math.sqrt(disc)) / 2
l2 = (tr + math.sqrt(disc)) / 2
print(l1)
print(l2)

traps: Do not stop at independent eigenvectors. Normalize every vector; Q must satisfy QᵀQ = I.
For a repeated eigenvalue, independent eigenvectors may not be orthogonal. Apply Gram-Schmidt inside that eigenspace.
Match the column order of Q to the diagonal order of D.
A non-symmetric real matrix can have complex eigenvalues; the real symmetric guarantee does not apply.

quiz.q: State the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices.
quiz.a: Every eigenvalue is real; eigenvectors from different eigenvalues are orthogonal; there is an orthonormal eigenbasis.

quiz.q: Why are eigenvectors from different eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix orthogonal?
quiz.a: For symmetric A, (Ax)ᵀy = xᵀ(Ay). With Ax = λx and Ay = μy, λxᵀy = μxᵀy. If λ ≠ μ, then xᵀy = 0.

quiz.q: For A = [[3, 1], [1, 3]], find the eigenvalues and an orthogonal Q with QᵀAQ = D.
A real symmetric 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues 2, 2, 5. What must you do inside the eigenspace for 2, and why?
quiz.a: Apply Gram-Schmidt to the basis of that eigenspace, then normalize. Independent eigenvectors for the repeated eigenvalue need not be orthogonal; Q needs orthonormal columns.
A square matrix Q with QᵀQ = I, equivalently Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ.

quiz.q: If Q is orthogonal, what is Q⁻¹?
Can a real symmetric matrix have eigenvalues 1 and 1+i? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix is real, so 1+i cannot occur.

beyond: Not for the exam. In data science, orthogonal diagonalization of a covariance matrix is principal component analysis: Q gives the new axes and D gives variances. In structural engineering, the same calculation gives vibration modes of a symmetric stiffness matrix. In quantum mechanics, Hermitian matrices play the role of real symmetric matrices, with complex inner products. Search for “principal component analysis eigenvector” and “spectral theorem symmetric matrix”. Numerical libraries compute this with QR iteration rather than by hand.
